title: Slow Reveal Graphs Are Awesome
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane advocates for 'slow reveal graphs' -- a classroom statistics routine developed by Jenna Laib in which a graph is revealed incrementally (shape only, then axes, then full context) with students noticing and predicting at each stage. Kane argues that school statistics typically shows students a narrow slice of what graphs look like in the real world, creating gaps -- one of his students thought a horizontal bar graph was 'facing the wrong way' because she had only ever seen vertical ones. The slow reveal technique exposes students to diverse, real-world graphs and generates genuine curiosity: discussions about whether George Washington could have met a Greenland shark still alive today, about ostrich locomotion, about Antarctic geography. Kane's broader argument is that learning things is intrinsically good -- that statistics class should give students a rich, broad conception of how data is represented in the world, not just practice with the simplest graph types. The routine is described as free, easy to implement via slowrevealgraphs.com, and accessible to teachers in any math classroom.
points: School statistics typically exposes students to a narrow slice of graph types, creating blind spots; a student who thought a horizontal bar graph was 'facing the wrong way' illustrates how limited classroom exposure produces limited graph literacy for the real world.

The slow reveal structure -- show shape, then axes, then full context with prediction at each stage -- creates genuine cognitive engagement and curiosity that standard graph instruction does not, and the routine is equally accessible to students who are quiet in regular math class.

Learning things is intrinsically good: Kane explicitly rejects the need to justify graph curiosity with future career utility -- knowing about long-lived Greenland sharks or Antarctic geography is worthwhile because 'learning things is good.'

The students who are most engaged by slow reveal graph discussions are often the students who are quiet and reserved in other parts of math class -- the format surfaces a different kind of engagement than conventional mathematics instruction.

The routine is easy to steal: slowrevealgraphs.com provides pre-made slide decks with built-in progressive reveals and a huge library of real-world graphs, requiring only minutes of teacher preparation per lesson.
quotes: Some areas of math are structured in a linear way. Addition should be learned before multiplication. Quadratics should be learned before higher-order polynomials. But not all math is nice and neat and linear, and statistics is particularly resistant to that linear structure.

I asked my students what they noticed. They made a few observations. One student said, 'it's facing the wrong way.' In school math, we tend to only show students a very small slice of what graphs can look like.
Statistics in school often misses the forest for the trees. Of all the math I teach, graphs are one of the pieces of math students will interact with most outside the math classroom.

My district, like a lot of districts, has deemphasized science and social studies in elementary school. That's a shame for a lot of reasons, and one is that students just don't know much about the world.

The conversations we have about slow reveal graphs have shown me how hungry students are to learn about the world. Sometimes we end up on a tangent discussing whether George Washington could have met a Greenland shark that is still alive today.

I do not care in the slightest whether a student will use their newfound knowledge of long-lived Greenland sharks in a future job. That's not the point. The point is to learn things, because learning things is good.
